# Dimensioning Rules {#dimensioningrules} ## Learning Objectives {-} By the end of this chapter, you will be able to: - Apply fundamental dimensioning rules according to ASME Y14.5 standards - Select appropriate dimension placement for clarity and manufacturability - Use proper extension lines, dimension lines, and leaders - Dimension common features including holes, arcs, and angles - Avoid common dimensioning errors ::: {.callout-think} **Before You Read:** Look at any mechanical part near you. How would you communicate its exact size to someone who needs to manufacture it? What measurements would be most important? ::: ## Introduction to Dimensioning Dimensioning is the process of adding size and location information to engineering drawings. Proper dimensioning ensures that parts can be manufactured exactly as the designer intended. ::: {.callout-industry} **Industry Connection:** NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter was lost in 1999 because one team's software reported thruster impulse in pound-force seconds while the navigation software expected newton seconds. The same kind of unit mix-up happens on drawings: a dimension of 25 means something very different in millimetres and in inches. Stating the units, and following one set of dimensioning rules, prevents such costly mistakes. ::: ## Elements of a Dimension A dimension is made of a few standard line types, all drawn thin so that they do not compete with the visible outline of the part: * **Extension lines** carry a feature out of the view. They start with a small visible **gap** (about 1.5 mm) from the part and run about **3 mm past** the last dimension line. * **Dimension lines** run between the extension lines and end in **arrowheads** that touch the extension lines. The number sits in a break in the line (ASME) or above it (ISO). * **Leaders** connect a note or a size callout to a feature. A leader to a hole or arc is drawn radially, so that if extended it would pass through the **centre**. It starts with a short horizontal shoulder at the note. * **Centre lines** (long–short dashes) mark the axis of holes and cylinders. A centre line may be extended and used as an extension line; it does not need a gap. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Elements of a dimension on a plate with one hole (mm): extension lines start with a small gap from the part and run a little past the dimension line; smaller dimensions sit closer to the part; the hole is located at its centre and sized with a leader in its circular view.](01-02-Dimensioning_files/figure-html/fig-dimension-elements-1.png){#fig-dimension-elements fig-align='center' width=864} ::: ::: ## Basic Dimensioning Rules (ASME Y14.5) 1. **Dimension each feature once.** A dimension repeated in a second view will contradict the first one the day only one of them is revised. 2. **Do not over-dimension.** In a chain of dimensions whose total is also given, leave one link out, or show it in parentheses as a *reference dimension*; otherwise the tolerances cannot all be met at once. 3. **Dimension in the view that shows the shape most clearly** (the characteristic view): a hole's diameter in the view where it appears as a circle, a slot's width where its outline is seen. 4. **Never dimension to hidden lines.** Use a visible edge, or add a section view that makes the feature visible. 5. **Place dimensions outside the view** where possible, with the **smaller dimensions closest to the part** and the larger ones outside them. Then extension lines never cross dimension lines. 6. **Dimension lines should not cross** each other or other lines. Extension lines may cross each other and visible lines when there is no other way. 7. **Locate holes by their centres**, not by their edges, and give their size with a diameter symbol: Ø12. Arcs are sized with a radius: R8. 8. **Choose dimensions from the part's function.** Measure from the surfaces that locate the part in the assembly (later, its datums), not from whatever edge was convenient to draw. 9. **State the units.** A drawing is all millimetres or all inches, with a note in the title block. Metric values below 1 get a leading zero (0.5, not .5); inch values drop it (.50). The full zero and decimal-place rules are in the Tolerances chapter. 10. **Use standard symbols and abbreviations** (Ø, R, ⌴ counterbore, ⌵ countersink, ↧ depth) so that anyone can read the drawing. ## Try it yourself {#sec-tryit-dimensioning} ```{=html}
``` ## Key Takeaways {-} - Dimensions should be placed for maximum clarity - Each dimension should appear only once on a drawing - Dimensions should relate to functional requirements - Standard symbols and conventions ensure universal understanding ::: {.callout-check} **Quick Check:** What is the difference between an extension line and a dimension line? Why is it important not to dimension to hidden lines? :::
